[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: 'the biggest so far' starts from nothing, i.e. 0, because everyday quantities are positive. Rule: the running maximum must start at a value no data can be below (Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY, Integer.MIN_VALUE) or at the first element, so that the first value read replaces it.
[1] misconception (M) -> ExtremeStartsAtZero: wrong rule: The running maximum can always start at 0. Right rule: Start the running maximum at the most negative possible value (Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY, or the smallest int) so that the first value read replaces it.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> ExtremeStartsAtZero: Points to LT: on each pass, compare a[i] with max and assign max = a[i] only if a[i] is larger. Inconsistent application: max is overwritten without the comparison on some passes, or compared with a stale value. (here mixing in: "The running maximum can always start at 0")

[0] names_the_element (N): Identity: a running maximum (or minimum), a variable holding the largest (smallest) value seen so far in a pass over the data; Sajaniemi's most-wanted holder.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Declarative: double max = Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY; for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) if (a[i] > max) max = a[i];.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Sequencing: initialize max before the loop; in each pass evaluate a[i] > max, and if it is true assign max = a[i]; read max only after the loop ends.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Result: the largest element (of the element type). For an empty array (or no input) max stays at its start value: NEGATIVE_INFINITY, or MIN_VALUE for int.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): State transition: one pass changes max only when a[i] > max; otherwise nothing changes.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): The maximum is found in one traversal, keeping the largest value seen so far, starting from Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Both make one pass over the values with one variable kept across passes. An accumulator (gatherer role) combines every value into it (sum += a[i]), so it starts at the identity 0.0; a running extreme (most-wanted holder) replaces it only when a better value is found (if (a[i] > max) max = a[i]), so it starts at Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY or the first value.
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan/role: most-wanted holder (Sajaniemi). It finds the extreme in one pass with constant extra memory; the same plan tracks the minimum with <.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> ExtremeStartsAtZero: Conservation: replacing > by >= keeps the maximum value but changes which tied position is the last one recorded. Remembering the index of the extreme instead of its value conserves the specification.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Applicability: use a running extreme when only the max or min (or its position) is needed, in a single pass. For further facts such as how many items equal the maximum, keep the data (an array) and make a second pass.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The start value must not exceed every possible data value. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: max starts at 0 (or Double.MIN_VALUE, which is the smallest positive double) and all data are negative, so the result is the start value
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Update only when the new value beats the current extreme. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: the comparison is reversed (a[i] < max), so the minimum is found, or max = a[i] is unconditional, so the last value is found

wrong: The running maximum can always start at 0. | right: Start the running maximum at the most negative possible value (Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY, or the smallest int), so that the first value read replaces it.

Both make one pass over the values with one variable kept across passes. An accumulator (gatherer role) combines every value into it (sum += a[i]), so it starts at the identity 0.0; a running extreme (most-wanted holder) replaces it only when a better value is found (if (a[i] > max) max = a[i]), so it starts at Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY or the first value.
The running maximum is found by traversing the array once, keeping the largest value seen so far (starting from Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY).
